what_its_for: Cetuximab is a cancer medicine used to treat certain types of head and neck cancer and a type of colorectal cancer (cancer of the colon or rectum). It works by blocking a protein called EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor) that helps cancer cells grow and divide. By blocking this protein, cetuximab slows or stops cancer growth.
how_to_take: Cetuximab is NOT a pill you take at home. It is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it is slowly dripped into your vein through a needle or IV line at a hospital, clinic, or infusion center. A trained healthcare professional will always give you this medicine. Each infusion usually takes about 1 to 2 hours. You will be watched closely during and after your infusion for any reactions. Before your first infusion, you may be given antihistamine medicine (like diphenhydramine/Benadryl) to help prevent allergic reactions.
dosing: Your doctor will calculate your dose based on your body size (height and weight). The typical starting dose is 400 mg per square meter of body surface area for the first infusion, followed by weekly maintenance doses of 250 mg per square meter. Your doctor may adjust your dose depending on how you respond to treatment or if you have side effects. Always follow the schedule your cancer care team gives you.
missed_dose: Because cetuximab is given at a medical facility, your healthcare team will schedule all of your appointments. If you need to miss or reschedule an appointment, call your doctor or infusion center as soon as possible. Do not try to skip doses or stop treatment on your own without talking to your doctor first, as this could make your treatment less effective.
storage: Cetuximab is stored and prepared by healthcare professionals at the clinic or hospital. You do not store this medicine at home. The prepared infusion solution should be kept at room temperature and used within a certain time frame by your care team. If you are ever given a vial to take home for any reason (which is very rare), store it in a refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze it.
what_to_avoid: Sun exposure: Cetuximab can make your skin very sensitive to the sun. Avoid prolonged sun exposure, use sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher, wear protective clothing and hats when outdoors, and avoid tanning beds. Skin irritants: Avoid harsh soaps, alcohol-based skin products, or anything that irritates your skin, as this medicine often causes acne-like skin rashes. Live vaccines: Do not receive any live vaccines (such as MMR, chickenpox, or nasal flu spray) while on cetuximab without asking your doctor first. Pregnancy: Avoid becoming pregnant during treatment and for at least 2 months after your last dose, as this medicine can harm an unborn baby.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: sudden difficulty breathing, shortness of breath, or wheezing during or after your infusion (possible serious allergic reaction); chest pain or tightness; severe skin rash, blistering, or peeling; signs of infection such as fever over 100.4°F (38°C), chills, or unusual warmth or redness; severe diarrhea or stomach pain; coughing up blood; sudden vision changes or eye pain; swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat; or weakness or numbness on one side of the body. Also tell your doctor about any new or worsening symptoms between appointments.
when_it_works: Cetuximab does not work overnight. It may take several weeks to months before you or your doctor can tell if the treatment is helping. Your doctor will check your progress with regular tests, scans, and blood work. Keep all of your scheduled appointments even if you feel well. Do not stop treatment unless your doctor tells you to.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Cetuximab can harm an unborn baby. Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 2 months after your last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for 2 months after your last dose. Elderly patients (65 and older): Older adults can receive cetuximab, but may need closer monitoring for side effects. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have any kidney or liver issues, as this may affect how well your body handles the medicine. Skin conditions: If you already have a skin condition, let your doctor know before starting treatment, as cetuximab commonly causes acne-like rashes and dry skin that may require special care.
